notes: Named for a Great Grandmother
Lord of Riverhead. Father of four sons: Aldous (heir), Renard, Cadmus, and Osbert. His fourth son Osbert's line would fall on hard times.
Wife of Lord Aldwin. From House Tillbrook, the farming vassals.
Lord of Riverhead. Eldest son who inherited. Father of Faraday, Kellam, and Emmeris.
Wife of Lord Aldous. From House Reedham of the marshlands.
Second son of Lord Aldwin. Respectable but died without significant issue.
Third son of Lord Aldwin. Unremarkable life, served the house loyally.
Fourth and youngest son of Lord Aldwin. His line fell on hard times. Grandfather of Harmond the Grasper.

Lord of Riverhead. Military-minded man with unmatched strategic ability and experience in the current Wilfrey family. Veteran of many campaigns and battles. The Breakmount Wilfreys have relied on him heavily and he has been recompensed with extended land claims and marriages for his children into the Breakmount line.
Lady of Riverhead. Wife of Lord Faraday. From House Millward, the miller lords sworn to Riverhead. A practical woman who manages the household with efficiency.

Younger brother of Lord Faraday. Married to Bronnis Wilfrey of Breakmount (ID 42) - one of the reward marriages for Faraday's military service. Manages the estates while his brother focuses on military matters.
Sister of Lord Faraday. Married to House Ironfell of the Marchlands, cementing a military alliance that has served both houses well.
Only son of Osbert (4th son of Aldwin). Has struggled financially and lives in reduced circumstances at Riverhead. Not quite poor but definitely not prosperous. Father of Harmond the Grasper.
Heir to Riverhead. Eldest son of Lord Faraday. Married to Grisella Salter, daughter of the Lord of the Scorch (Dust Bowl). A capable administrator who learned logistics from managing the food stores.
Wife of Eldric, heir to Riverhead. Eldest daughter of House Salter of the Scorch. The marriage alliance creates economic interdependence: Riverhead's water and food for the Scorch's salt.
Daughter of Lord Faraday. Married to Kirk Wilfrey of Breakmount (ID 186) - a reward marriage for Faraday's military service. Lives primarily at Breakmount with her husband's family.
Youngest daughter of Lord Faraday. Married to House Bridger of Longford, securing river trade routes and toll income downstream.
Son of Kellam Wilfrey and Bronnis Wilfrey of Breakmount. Married to a daughter of House Reedham. Serves as his uncle Faraday's master of stores.
Wife of Rennick Wilfrey. From House Reedham of the marshlands.
Daughter of Kellam Wilfrey and Bronnis Wilfrey of Breakmount. Unmarried. Known for her sharp mind and sharper tongue.

THE GRASPER. Son of Corvin, grandson of Osbert, great-grandson of Aldwin. Fourth son of a second son of the fourth son of a lord. Ambitious and capable but with no prospects. His line fell on hard times and he is now grasping for any role that might bring him back into the fold. Hungry for recognition and advancement.
Eldest son of Eldric. Heir to the heir of Riverhead. Currently fostering at Breakmount as tradition demands.

Second son of Eldric. BETROTHED to Marta Wilfrey of Breakmount (ID 26, b.2008), daughter of Mychal. The betrothal is another reward for Lord Faraday's service to Breakmount. Marriage expected when both come of age.
Daughter of Eldric. Youngest child of the heir to Riverhead.
Son of Rosmund Wilfrey of Riverhead and Kirk Wilfrey of Breakmount. Lives at Breakmount with his father's family but maintains ties to Riverhead through his mother.
Daughter of Rosmund Wilfrey of Riverhead and Kirk Wilfrey of Breakmount.
Son of Rennick Wilfrey and Tamsyn Reedham. Named for his mother's family's marshy homeland.

Lord of House Wilfriver. Slippery and charming, he maintains the house's legitimate barge trade while suspected of running smuggling operations through retainers and unsavoury types. Never caught. His political standing is moderate - useful to the main house - but his personal repute is poor.
Wife of Lord Goram Wilfriver. From House Tillbrook, the farming vassals. Married into Wilfriver before their reputation soured; she maintains the house's respectability as best she can.
Heir to House Wilfriver. More openly involved in 'the trade' than his father. Rumored to personally oversee certain shipments that move by night.
Daughter of Lord Goram Wilfriver. Serves as the respectable face of the house. Manages their legitimate trade dealings and desperately seeks a good marriage to improve the family's standing.

Lord of House Ironfell of the Marchlands. Husband of Emmeris Wilfrey (Faraday's sister). A hardened military man who shares Lord Faraday's martial temperament. Their alliance has been mutually beneficial.
Heir to House Bridger of Longford. Husband of Lysara Wilfrey. A practical merchant-lord who sees the value in the Riverhead alliance for controlling river trade.
Lord of House Wilfson. Father of Baudin, Adelise, Nivette, and Colard. Died peacefully with clean succession to Baudin, but Baudin died shortly after in The Scandal of 1776.

Wife of Lord Faramund Wilfson. Born to House Wilfrey of Riverhead as 2nd daughter under The Old Right practice. Outlived her husband and witnessed the tragedy of The Scandal. Saw one son kill another.

Eldest son of Faramund. Briefly Lord of House Wilfson after his father's death. Killed by his younger brother Colard in a duel during The Scandal of 1776. His death led to the founding of House Wilson by his sister Nivette.

Daughter of Faramund Wilfson. Married Aldric Wilfrey of Breakmount before The Scandal, maintaining a Wilfson connection to the main house untainted by the kinslaying. Lived long and witnessed the aftermath.

Daughter of Faramund Wilfson. Fled with her betrothed Lennis of Fourhearth after The Scandal of 1776 to found House Wilson. Co-founder of the broken branch that received Crown recognition in 1785 to break from Wilfrey Drith authority.

The Kinslayer. Younger son of Faramund who killed his brother Baudin in a duel during The Scandal of 1776. Became Lord and preserved the house through 36 years of grim, dedicated service. Named his heir Baudric - a variant of Baudin - a controversial choice that divided the house.

Wife of Colard Wilfson. Born to House Wilfrey of Bramblehall. Their marriage in 1778, two years after The Scandal, was a gesture of reconciliation - Bramblehall forgave the chaos that originated from their seat.

Lord of House Wilfson 1812-1848. Named in memory of his uncle Baudin - a controversial choice. Some saw it as honoring the dead; others as tempting fate. Never discussed the matter publicly. First lord to marry outside the Wilfrey web after The Scandal.
Second son of Colard. The 'spare heir' - married into House Goff. His line continues but not in direct succession. Named to honor his grandfather Faramund.
Daughter of Colard Wilfson. Married into House Wilfern, the Breakmount cadet branch.

Wife of Lord Baudric Wilfson. Born to House Salter of the Scorch - a deliberate choice to bring fresh blood from outside the Wilfrey web after The Scandal. This began a pattern of alternating between Wilfrey marriages and outside alliances.
Lord of House Wilfson 1848-1878. His name was a variant of Colard - the kinslayer redeemed through generations of loyal service. Third generation after The Scandal.

Daughter of Baudric Wilfson. Named to honor grandmother Ermeline. Married into House Wilfrey of Fourhearth, restoring connection to Lennis's old seat - a symbolic gesture given that Lennis's departure created House Wilson.
Third child of Baudric Wilfson. Named to honor his mother Giseline. Never married. Became a noted administrator, served as Fosterreeve for 30 years.

Wife of Lord Coland Wilfson. Born to House Thornbury of the eastern reaches - a Drith-level landed family known for horse breeding. Marriage represented diversification outside the Wilfrey web while maintaining appropriate standing for a cadet house.
Lord of House Wilfson 1878-1905. Fourth generation after The Scandal. Returned to traditional Wilfrey alliance by marrying into Riverhead.
Daughter of Coland Wilfson. Married into House Athelmere, establishing the connection that continues to the present day with Jon Wilfson's marriage to Saelis Athelmere.
Third child of Coland Wilfson. Named as a variant honoring grandfather Colard while remaining distinct. Never married. Served as Fosterbookman in the fostering system.
Wife of Lord Berin Wilfson. Born to House Wilfrey of Riverhead - a return to traditional alliance four generations after The Scandal.
Lord of House Wilfson 1905-1932. Named to honor the ancestral founder Faramund with slightly varied spelling. Fifth generation after The Scandal.
Daughter of Berin Wilfson. Named after her mother Celisse. Married into House Goff.
Third child of Berin Wilfson. Pursued a military career, never inherited.
Wife of Lord Farmund Wilfson. Born to House Cawdry, a minor house - an appropriate practical match for a cadet branch.
Lord of House Wilfson 1932-1960. Sixth generation after The Scandal.
Daughter of Farmund Wilfson. Married into House Eldwick (motto: 'What Was, Remains') - a practical match for a cadet daughter.
Third child of Farmund Wilfson. Died young at 24 - likely in war or by accident.
Wife of Lord Colbert Wilfson. Born to House Parlin, a minor house - another practical match maintaining appropriate standing.

Lord of House Wilfson 1960-1985. Seventh generation after The Scandal. Father of Jon Wilfson. His marriage to Loveline of Breakmount represented full restoration of House Wilfson's position - no longer marked by kinslaying, fully trusted.
Daughter of Colbert Wilfson. Married into House Wentburn.
Third child of Colbert Wilfson. Unmarried. Served in the fostering system as Fostersteward.

Wife of Lord Bauric Wilfson. Born to House Wilfrey of Breakmount - this marriage represented the full restoration of House Wilfson's position after generations of rebuilding trust following The Scandal.
Daughter of Bauric Wilfson, sister of Jon and Betts. Married into House Ferncross, a minor house.

Heir of Jon Wilfson. Named for the ancestor who died in The Scandal of 1776 - 250 years later, the name is finally reclaimed. A sign that House Wilfson has fully processed the trauma of the kinslaying.
Daughter of Jon Wilfson and Saelis Athelmere. Named as a variation of her mother's name.
Daughter of House Dundas. A practical match for the heir of House Wilfson, bringing quiet competence rather than grand alliance. Married Jon Wilfson in 1998.

Founder and first Lord of House Wilson. Born Lennis Wilfrey, heir to Fourhearth Castle. Fled north with Nivette Wilfson after The Scandal of 1776. Received royal grant of lands at Grantholm ~1778, with formal Crown recognition of House Wilson in 1785. Chose the name 'Wilson' — close enough to 'Wilfson' to claim the lineage, different enough to mark independence. Ruled ~1778-1815.

Second Lord of House Wilson (1815-1850). First child of Lennis and Nivette, named for the uncle who died defending their marriage — Baudin Wilfson. This began the Wilson tradition: every firstborn son bears the name Baudin. Born shortly after settlement at Grantholm.

Second child of Lennis and Nivette Wilson. Named as a feminine form honoring Colard Wilfson — the brother who killed Baudin. Lennis reportedly said: 'Colard did what he believed was right. We do not hate him for it.' Married Rodric Ashford ~1798, the first Wilson daughter to wed. House Ashford's acceptance helped legitimize the exiled family among northern nobility.
Third child of Lennis and Nivette Wilson. Named to honor Nivette's father Faramund Wilfson. The 'spare heir' — if something happened to Baudin, the line would continue.

Fourth child of Lennis and Nivette Wilson. Named as a feminine form of her father's name. Married Aldric Fenwick ~1805. House Fenwick's ancient lineage (founded ~980) accepting a Wilson bride reinforced that House Wilson was northern now, not Wilfrey.

Wife of Baudin Wilson I. Born to House Northmere, an ancient Northern Crown House seated at Merehall. Married ~1800. The first bride to join the exiled house from the northern nobility, helping legitimize House Wilson among their new neighbors.

Husband of Colardine Wilson. Son of House Ashford, a minor but respectable Northern Crown House seated at Ashford Hall. Married ~1798. His family's acceptance of a Wilson bride helped legitimize the exiled house among northern nobility.

Husband of Lenniselle Wilson. Son of House Fenwick, one of the most ancient Northern Crown Houses (founded ~980), seated at Fenwick Keep. Married ~1805. The Fenwicks' deep roots predating the Wilfrey ascendancy gave this match particular significance.
Third Lord of House Wilson (1850-1875). Baudin Wilson II, continuing the naming tradition. Married Isolda Kingsward ~1828, reinforcing House Wilson's legitimacy as a Crown-favored house.
Second child of Baudin Wilson I and Cereline. Named to honor grandmother Nivette. Married Beric Northmere ~1825, creating a reciprocal bond with House Northmere (her mother's birth house).
Third child of Baudin Wilson I and Cereline. Named to honor his mother's name.

Wife of Baudin Wilson II. Born to House Kingsward, a Northern Crown House seated at Wardkeep, guarding the northern royal road. Married ~1828. The Kingsward connection reinforced House Wilson's legitimacy as a Crown-favored house.
Husband of Niveline Wilson. Son of House Northmere. Married ~1825, creating a double bond between Wilson and Northmere (Cereline Northmere had married Baudin I).
Fourth Lord of House Wilson (1875-1905). Baudin Wilson III. Married Hamelina Granford ~1855.
Second child of Baudin Wilson II and Isolda. Married Garen Kingsward ~1853, strengthening the Wilson-Kingsward bond.
Third child of Baudin Wilson II and Isolda. Named to honor founder Lennis.

Wife of Baudin Wilson III. Born to House Granford, a Northern Crown House seated at Granford Keep amid rich farmland. Married ~1855. Her daughter Hameline Wilson later married Tormund Granford (~1882), creating a double bond.
Husband of Iselde Wilson. Son of House Kingsward. Married ~1853.
Fifth Lord of House Wilson (1905-1935). Baudin Wilson IV. Married Aureline Croftmoor ~1885.
Second child of Baudin Wilson III and Hamelina. Married Tormund Granford ~1882, creating a double bond with House Granford (her mother was born Granford).
Third child of Baudin Wilson III and Hamelina.

Wife of Baudin Wilson IV. Born to House Croftmoor, a Northern Crown House seated at Moorstead in the remote moorlands. Married ~1885. Her daughter Croftine Wilson later married Aldwin Croftmoor (~1916), strengthening the bond.
Husband of Hameline Wilson. Son of House Granford. Married ~1882.
Sixth Lord of House Wilson (1935-1965). Baudin Wilson V. Married Doreline Helmward ~1918 — a later marriage, age 30, perhaps due to the wars or military service of that era.
Second child of Baudin Wilson IV and Aureline.
Third child of Baudin Wilson IV and Aureline. Married Aldwin Croftmoor ~1916, creating a double bond with House Croftmoor (her mother was born Croftmoor).

Wife of Baudin Wilson V. Born to House Helmward, a Northern Crown House of military tradition seated at Helm Castle on the northern border. Married ~1918. Her daughter Helmina Wilson later married Roderick Helmward (~1948).
Husband of Croftine Wilson. Son of House Croftmoor. Married ~1916.
Seventh Lord of House Wilson (1965-1995). Baudin Wilson VI. Married Sireline Blackmoor ~1948.
Second child of Baudin Wilson V and Doreline.
Third child of Baudin Wilson V and Doreline. Married Roderick Helmward ~1948, creating a double bond with House Helmward (her mother was born Helmward).

Wife of Baudin Wilson VI. Born to House Blackmoor, an ancient and insular Northern Crown House seated at Blackmoor Hall in the dark peatlands. Married ~1948. Her daughter Moraine Wilson later married Cedric Blackmoor (~1978).
Husband of Helmina Wilson. Son of House Helmward. Married ~1948.

Eighth Lord of House Wilson (1995-present). Baudin Wilson VII, the current Lord. Married Eveline Stormcrest ~1975. When asked about the Baudin naming tradition, Wilsons typically respond: 'We remember Baudin. We always will.'
Second child of Baudin Wilson VI and Sireline.
Third child of Baudin Wilson VI and Sireline. Married Cedric Blackmoor ~1978, creating a double bond with House Blackmoor (her mother was born Blackmoor).
Wife of Baudin Wilson VII, current Lady of House Wilson. Born to House Stormcrest, a seafaring Northern Crown House seated at Cresthold on the northern coast. Married ~1975.
Husband of Moraine Wilson. Son of House Blackmoor. Married ~1978.
Heir to House Wilson. Baudin Wilson VIII, ninth generation to bear the name. Not yet succeeded. Married Marelisse Thornwick ~2005. This match elevated House Thornwick's status considerably.
Second child of Baudin Wilson VII and Eveline. Married Garrett Stormcrest ~2005, creating a double bond with House Stormcrest (her mother was born Stormcrest).
Third child of Baudin Wilson VII and Eveline. Named to honor founder Lennis.

Wife of Baudin Wilson VIII. Born to House Thornwick, the youngest of the Northern Crown Houses (founded ~1920), seated at Thornwick Manor. Married ~2005. This match elevated House Thornwick's status considerably.
Husband of Evelind Wilson. Son of House Stormcrest. Married ~2005.

Heir to Baudin Wilson VIII. Baudin Wilson IX, tenth generation to bear the name. Continuing the tradition established when Lennis and Nivette named their firstborn for the uncle who gave his life for their marriage.
Second child of Baudin Wilson VIII and Marelisse. Too young to marry.

Lord of Bramblehall during The Scandal of 1776. Father of six daughters — legendarily inflated to 'ten' as the beauty of their retainers and companions became confused with the daughters themselves over generations of retelling. Also father of two sons, Aldric and Borsward, born as twins alongside two of his daughters. Brought the matter of Raylegh and Lennis before the Riverhead Council. Watched his daughter Giseline marry the kinslayer Colard Wilfson in 1778 as a gesture of reconciliation. Never spoke publicly of Raylegh's fate after the scandal.

Wife of Lord Constann of Bramblehall, born of House Wilfrey of Riverhead. Mother of eight children — six daughters and two sons. The 'ten daughters' legend absorbed the beauty of her daughters' retainers and companions, inflating the count over generations of storytelling. Her son Aldric was eldest of all her children but entirely overshadowed by his sisters' fame.

The eldest child of Constann, born alongside his twin sister Constance. So overshadowed by his six beautiful sisters that history barely remembers him. He inherited Bramblehall upon his father's death ~1790 and ruled quietly for 25 years. Where his sisters were legendary, Aldric was steady — exactly what Bramblehall needed after the scandal.
Second son of Constann, twin with Belisent. Even more forgotten than Aldric. Married locally and his descendants were absorbed into the woodland cadet branches.

Eldest daughter of Lord Constann, twin with Aldric. Named for her father. Married Renfric Wilfrey of Breakmount ~1765 — the most advantageous match of all the daughters, binding Bramblehall to the paramount Wilfrey seat.
Second daughter of Lord Constann, named for her mother Florine. Married Dunric Wilfrey of Fourhearth ~1768, binding Bramblehall to the maritime seat.
Third daughter of Lord Constann, twin with Borsward. Married Godfric Hendry ~1770, extending Bramblehall's reach to House Hendry.
Fourth daughter of Lord Constann. Married Vesmund Vespen ~1774, deepening the feudal bond between Bramblehall and its sworn house, House Vespen.

Fifth daughter of Lord Constann. Her night with Lennis Wilfrey — disguised as a serving wench — triggered The Scandal of 1776 that led to the founding of House Wilson. After the scandal, her father honoured the original betrothal to the Old Knight. She bore him twin boys before dying in childbirth, as she had feared. The twins' fate is unknown — whether they lived or died, and what names they bore, has been lost to time. Whether Lennis knew her identity that night, whether she planned it, and what truly happened remain among the great unanswered questions of Wilfrey history.

Husband of Constance, daughter of Lord Constann. Son of House Wilfrey of Breakmount. Married ~1765. The most advantageous match among the six daughters' marriages, binding Bramblehall directly to the paramount seat.
Husband of Floriselle, daughter of Lord Constann. Son of House Wilfrey of Fourhearth. Married ~1768.
Husband of Belisent, daughter of Lord Constann. Eldest son of Lord Hendry. Married ~1770.
Husband of Adelise, daughter of Lord Constann. Heir to House Vespen, sworn to Bramblehall. Married ~1774.

The wealthy, elderly knight to whom Raylegh was betrothed. His true name has been deliberately obscured by history — the Bramblehall people chose to forget it, perhaps out of pity, perhaps out of shame. He married Raylegh after the scandal as originally agreed. She bore him twin boys before dying in childbirth. He lived another seven years. What became of the boys after his death is unknown.

Wife of Lord Aldric of Bramblehall, born of House Wilfrey of Riverhead. Like her mother-in-law Florine, Bereline came from Riverhead — a political match befitting the heir of Bramblehall. The woodland marriage tradition among the broader population was well-established by this time, but the lord's heir was expected to look further afield.
Third Lord of Bramblehall (~1815-1845). Constann Wilfrey II, named for his grandfather. Married Elismere of Fourhearth — maintaining the expectation that the heir married outside the woodland.
Daughter of Lord Aldric of Bramblehall.
Youngest son of Lord Aldric of Bramblehall.

Wife of Constann Wilfrey II, born of House Wilfrey of Fourhearth. A Fourhearth bride — maintaining the tradition that the heir, at least, married outside the woodland. Her connection to Fourhearth strengthened the maritime trade that even insular Bramblehall relied upon.
Fourth Lord of Bramblehall (~1845-1875). The first lord's heir to marry woodland — his choice of Mirette Wilfbark raised eyebrows but cemented the woodland branches' loyalty for a generation.
Daughter of Constann Wilfrey II of Bramblehall.
Son of Constann Wilfrey II of Bramblehall.

Wife of Lord Aldwin of Bramblehall, born of House Wilfbark. The first woodland bride to marry a lord's heir at Bramblehall. While the broader Bramblehall population had long married within the woodland branches, an heir doing so was unusual and caused comment. But Aldwin was a man of the forest more than the court, and Mirette's family knew the deep wood better than anyone alive.

Fifth Lord of Bramblehall (~1875-1905). After his father Aldwin's woodland marriage, Miric married back outside — a Breakmount bride. Some saw this as a correction; others noted that Miric simply fell in love with the wrong woman for tradition's sake.
Daughter of Lord Aldwin of Bramblehall.
Wife of Lord Miric of Bramblehall, born of House Wilfrey of Breakmount. After Aldwin's woodland marriage, Miric married back outside — a Breakmount bride this time.
Sixth Lord of Bramblehall (~1905-1935). Married Hildeline of Riverhead — another bride from outside the forest, like Constann's own wife Florine three generations earlier.
Daughter of Lord Miric of Bramblehall.

Wife of Lord Borswin of Bramblehall, born of House Wilfrey of Riverhead. Another bride from outside the forest — Riverhead, like Constann's own wife Florine three generations earlier. The Riverhead connection remained strong.

Seventh Lord of Bramblehall (~1935-1965). Aldric Wilfrey II. Only the second lord's heir in Bramblehall's history to marry woodland — and the first in three generations. Like Aldwin before him, Aldric II was a man who felt more at home among the trees than in a great hall.
Son of Lord Borswin of Bramblehall.
Wife of Aldric Wilfrey II of Bramblehall, born of House Wilfbark. Only the second lord's heir in Bramblehall's history to marry woodland — and the first in three generations.
Son of Aldric Wilfrey II of Bramblehall.
Wife of Bors Wilfrey of Bramblehall, born of House Wilfbauer. The third lord to marry woodland, making it the most such marriages in living memory.

Daughter of Bors Wilfrey. Her marriage to Aldwin Athelmere transformed the relationship between Bramblehall and House Athelmere from purely feudal to familial. Mother of Elias Athelmere, current Lord Athelmere.

Husband of Woodina Wilfrey, daughter of Bors Wilfrey of Bramblehall. Father of Elias Athelmere, current Lord Athelmere. His marriage to Woodina deepened the bond between House Athelmere and Bramblehall from purely feudal to familial.

Wife of Lord Alec of Bramblehall, born of House Wilfbole. Her marriage was hasty — Bors's sudden death meant Alec needed to secure succession quickly. Alec is the first lord to follow a woodland marriage with another woodland marriage — two in a row being unprecedented.
Heir to Bramblehall. Named for his grandfather Bors. Current heir to Lord Alec.
Daughter of Lord Alec of Bramblehall.
Son of Lord Alec of Bramblehall.
Wife of Borsham Wilfrey, born of House Wilfbark. Continuing the woodland marriage tradition common among the broader Bramblehall population.
Son of Borsham Wilfrey of Bramblehall.
Daughter of Borsham Wilfrey of Bramblehall.

Head of House Wilfbauer and master of Bauerholt. The most outward-looking of the three woodland branch heads, Garmund manages the farming clearings that feed much of Bramblehall's population. Father of Aldmund.
Wife of Garmund Wilfbauer. Born locally in the Bramblehall woodlands.
Heir to Bauerholt. Son of Garmund Wilfbauer.

Head of House Wilfbole and master of Bolewood. A master woodcrafter whose joinery is sought across the region. The most traditional of the three woodland heads — he maintains the old forest rites that even Bramblehall has half-forgotten.
Wife of Torwin Wilfbole. Born locally in the Bramblehall woodlands.
Heir to Bolewood. Son of Torwin Wilfbole. Learning his father's craft.
Head of House Wilfbark and warden of Barkhollow. Chief hunter and tracker of the deep wood. Knows every path, clearing, and animal run in the forest. The most insular of the three woodland heads.
Wife of Aldhelm Wilfbark. Born locally in the Bramblehall deep woods.
Heir to Barkhollow. Son of Aldhelm Wilfbark. Already reckoned the best tracker of his generation.
Head of House Wilfsbane and master of Banehold. His house guards the high passes above the silver mines of Night Mountain — harsh country that breeds harsh men. A loyal vassal of Breakmount.
Wife of Merric Wilfsbane, born of House Wilfern. Marriage between the two Breakmount cadet branches strengthened both.
Heir to Banehold. Son of Merric Wilfsbane.
Daughter of Merric Wilfsbane.

Head of House Wilfour and master of Fourgate. His house controls the harbour entrance at Fourhearth — every vessel that enters or leaves passes under Wilfour eyes. A profitable position that makes them the wealthiest of Fourhearth's cadets.
Wife of Gareth Wilfour. A merchant's daughter who brought trade connections to the marriage.
Heir to Fourgate. Son of Gareth Wilfour. Already involved in the harbour trade.
Daughter of Gareth Wilfour.

Head of House Wilfsands and master of Sandholme. His house holds the tidal flats and sandbanks south of Fourhearth — salt-panning, shellfish, and salvage rights from wrecked vessels. Less wealthy than the Wilfours but more self-sufficient.
Wife of Rowan Wilfsands. A fisher's daughter from the coastal villages.
Heir to Sandholme. Son of Rowan Wilfsands. Knows the tides and sandbanks better than anyone his age.

Head of House Wilfmarsh and master of Fenholm. His house controls the marshy lowlands where the river broadens into wetlands — drainage, flood management, and eel-catching. Less prestigious than the Wilfrivers but more dependable. Where Wilfriver has moderate standing and ill repute, Wilfmarsh has low standing but good repute.
Wife of Godwin Wilfmarsh. Born in the fen villages along the river.
Heir to Fenholm. Son of Godwin Wilfmarsh.
Daughter of Godwin Wilfmarsh.

Bastard son of a younger Bramblehall Wilfrey — the first recorded Dunwilfrey at Bramblehall. Breakmount had its bastards, but the insular woodland people had kept their indiscretions quieter until Osbert's father acknowledged the boy publicly. Worked as a forester his whole life.
Bastard daughter of a Riverhead Wilfrey lord's younger son and a barge-woman. Acknowledged but never fully accepted at Riverhead. Lives on the river, like her mother.

Bastard son of a Fourhearth Wilfrey and a harbour-side tavern keeper. The first recorded Dunwilfrey at Fourhearth. Made a modest living as a chandler. His descendants, if any, likely live among the dockside communities.

Bastard son of a Wilfson lord's brother. The Wilfson name already carried the stain of the kinslaying — a bastard branch of a tainted house was doubly marginal. Cedwin worked the silver mines, as many Dunwilfson men did after him.

Bastard son of a Wilfern knight and a village woman from the western foothills. Acknowledged by his father but raised by his mother. The Wilfern cadets held a minor castle, and Beric was permitted to serve there as a man-at-arms — close to the family but never truly of it.

Bastard daughter of a Wilfriver man and a river trader's wife. The Wilfrivers are widely suspected of smuggling, and Halla's mother was likely involved in the barge trade. Acknowledged — the Wilfrivers are not proud enough to deny their blood, only proud enough to put their name on it.

Bastard son of an early Wilson lord's younger brother and a northern farmwoman. Even in exile, the Wilfrey blood ran hot. The Wilsons acknowledged Farren quietly — they had spent a century building legitimacy and a bastard was an inconvenience, not a scandal. He farmed near Grantholm his whole life.

Born to a woman of House Wilfrey of Fourhearth and a common sailor. Her mother was a younger daughter with no marriage prospects — the sailor was a passing indiscretion. But the Wilfrey name was too valuable to abandon. Cerys bore it her whole life as a Dumwilfrey — not quite Wilfrey, but close enough to open some doors and close others. Lived in the harbour communities of Fourhearth.

Born to a woman of House Wilfrey of Bramblehall and a travelling merchant. Dum-named bastards are rare — most children take their father's name. But in the Wilfrey context, the mother's name carries enough weight that some choose it deliberately. Annis grew up on the edges of Bramblehall's woodland communities, neither fully inside nor fully outside.

Second son of the Breakmount Wilfreys. Founded Bramblehall in 1176 after being granted Wyrmwood Forest and surrounding lands by the Crown for extraordinary military service. Made Drithen equal to Great Drithen. Formalized the Wood-Warden's Oath with the forest-folk he found already managing Wyrmwood, recognizing that partnership served better than conquest.

Eldest Steward of Haligdene. Has tended the sacred valley for thirty-two years. Leads the Midwinter delegation to Bramblehall and personally cuts the Mirellune stem for presentation. Deeply involved in thirren management. Traditionalist who believes the Wood-Warden's Oath must be honoured scrupulously. Grandfather of Theren Wythern.

Keeper of Greenweft. Skilled herbalist and healer who maintains the medicinal gardens of Wyrmwood. More open to outsiders than most Wytherns. Argues for a stronger negotiating position with Bramblehall — not breaking the Compact, but ensuring it evolves. Believes thirren management gives forest-folk leverage that should be used wisely.

Young steward who recently swore the Stewardship Oath at Haligdene. Grandson of Eldric Wythern. Represents the new generation questioning traditional isolation. Interested in formal trade partnerships with Bramblehall. Questions whether the Mustering-Right still serves forest-folk interests. His views create tension with his grandfather.

Influential voice among non-Wythern forest families of Wyrmwood. Skilled tracker, hunter, and expert thirren cultivator with knowledge equal to any Wythern. Argues that Wythern soft-leadership perpetuates unfair hierarchy. Advocates for rotating the Mirellune presentation among all forest-folk families. Significant support among younger forest-folk.
